prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Pearl Avenue runs past the high-school lot, Bends with the trolley tracks, and stops, cut off Before it has a chance to go two blocks, At Colonel McComsky Plaza. Berth’s Garage Is on the corner facing west, and there, Most days, you'll find Flick Webb, who helps Berth out. Flick stands tall among the idiot pumps— Five on a side, the old bubble-head style, Their rubber elbows hanging loose and low. One’s nostrils are two S’s, and his eyes An E and O. And one is squat, without A head at all—more of a football type. Once Flick played for the high-school team, the Wizards. He was good: in fact, the best. In ’46 He bucketed three hundred ninety points, A county record still. The ball loved Flick. I saw him rack up thirty-eight or forty In one home game. His hands were like wild birds. He never learned a trade, he just sells gas, Checks oil, and changes flats. Once in a while, As a gag, he dribbles an inner tube, But most of us remember anyway. His hands are fine and nervous on the lug wrench. It makes no difference to the lug wrench, though. Off work, he hangs around Mae’s Luncheonette. Grease-gray and kind of coiled, he plays pinball, Smokes those thin cigars, nurses lemon phosphates. Flick seldom says a word to Mae, just nods Beyond her face toward bright applauding tiers Of Necco Wafers, Nibs, and Juju Beads.

outputs.L2:
Pearl Avenue passes the high school grounds, curves alongside the streetcar rails, and then dead-ends at Colonel McComsky Plaza before extending even two blocks. On the west-facing corner stands Berth’s Garage, where Flick Webb can usually be found helping Berth.

Flick is tall beside the ten foolish-looking, old-fashioned gas pumps, arranged five to each side. They have rounded glass tops and rubber hoses drooping like slack arms. One pump seems to have a face made from two S-shaped nostrils and the letters E and O for eyes. Another is short and headless, shaped more like a football player.

Years ago, Flick played basketball for the high school Wizards. He was not merely talented but the finest player around. In 1946, he scored 390 points, a county record that remains unbroken. Flick seemed naturally matched to the basketball. The speaker once watched him score thirty-eight or perhaps forty points during a home game, his hands moving with the quick freedom of untamed birds.

Flick never acquired a skilled profession. Now he pumps gasoline, measures oil levels, and repairs flat tires. Occasionally, as a joke, he bounces an inner tube as though dribbling a ball, though the local people need no reminder of his former glory. His sensitive, restless hands handle the lug wrench expertly, but the tool itself is indifferent to his talent.

When his shift ends, Flick spends time at Mae’s Luncheonette. Wearing the gray grime of garage work and seeming tightly wound, he plays the pinball machine, smokes slender cigars, and slowly drinks lemon phosphates. He rarely speaks to Mae. Instead, he gives a nod past her toward the brightly colored rows of Necco Wafers, Nibs, and Juju Beads, which resemble cheering spectators in stadium seats.
outputs.L3:
Pearl Avenue comes to an end at Colonel McComsky Plaza, where Flick Webb works at Berth’s Garage. His present life is modest and routine, but he was once a celebrated athlete—the greatest basketball player his high school had ever known. In 1946, Flick set a county scoring record, earning admiration for his remarkable talent on the court.

That early success, however, did not lead to a lasting career. Flick never learned a trade, and his days are now spent selling gasoline, checking oil, and changing tires. His hands still retain something of their former quickness and precision, though they have also become nervous and restless. Once, those hands controlled a basketball with exceptional skill; now they grip a lug wrench, an unfeeling tool incapable of recognizing the talent they once displayed.

After work, Flick often goes to Mae’s Luncheonette, where he passes the time quietly. He plays pinball, smokes cigars, and stares at the colorful candy displays. In their bright rows and rounded shapes, he seems to glimpse an echo of his former glory—the crowds who once watched him play and rewarded his achievements with enthusiastic applause.
outputs.L4:
In John Updike’s poem “Ex-Basketball Player,” the narrator describes Flick Webb, a former high-school basketball star who now works at a gas station in his hometown. The setting immediately emphasizes the narrowness of Flick’s present life. Instead of moving toward a promising future, he remains close to the school where he once achieved fame, performing routine tasks such as pumping gas and checking oil. His ordinary surroundings contrast sharply with the excitement and admiration that defined his youth.

During his high-school career, Flick was an exceptional athlete. He set scoring records, impressed spectators, and seemed almost naturally suited to basketball. On the court, he possessed confidence, skill, and a clear sense of purpose. The vivid memories of his achievements show how completely his identity was shaped by the sport. Basketball gave him recognition and made him important within his community, but that success did not translate into opportunities or direction after graduation.

Flick’s present behavior suggests that he remains emotionally attached to his former glory. He spends his free time around games and machines that remind him of basketball, as though he is trying to preserve a connection to the period when he felt most alive. Yet he does not openly express regret or disappointment. His silence makes his situation more poignant because the reader must infer his longing from his habits and surroundings.

Through Flick’s story, the poem explores the temporary nature of youthful fame. Athletic talent can bring admiration and a strong identity, but those rewards may disappear quickly once school ends. Flick’s unrealized potential reveals how poorly early success may prepare a person for adulthood when it is not accompanied by broader goals or opportunities. His life therefore becomes a quiet warning: glory can be intense but brief, and someone who lives mainly through past achievements may struggle to find meaning in the present.

Pearl Avenue bends gently along the river, disappearing beneath a canopy of old maple trees. In the morning, sunlight glimmers on the wet pavement like scattered pearls, while cyclists follow the road’s quiet curves into town. Beyond the final bend stands a small blue house, its windows facing the water—a peaceful place where the avenue ends and the open countryside begins.
